content: The primary methods employed in the review process should be clearly outlined, with a particular emphasis on the validity, objectivity, and representativeness of the data collected. Additionally, the conduct of the review itself must be critically assessed to ensure its rigor and reliability. The findings of the review should begin with an evaluation of the overall impact of the program on key health outcomes, including incidence, prevalence, mortality, and morbidity. Specific findings can then be organized either by the program’s objectives or by its operational areas, as detailed in the relevant annex. When reporting and utilizing the findings of the review, the recommendations should be divided into two categories: overarching recommendations that address the program as a whole, and specific recommendations that pertain to particular programmatic areas or subsystems. These specific recommendations may also serve as extensions of the main recommendations. Annexes should provide additional information, such as the full terms of reference, details of individuals involved in the review (e.g., steering group members, review team, experts), supplementary data analyses, a list of interviewees, locations visited, documents reviewed, and the data collection tools utilized. The review team may also propose alternative formats for presenting the findings, such as slide presentations or summary brochures, to complement the full report. A national dialogue should follow the completion of the program review. This dialogue can be integrated into broader participatory processes related to development, the health sector, or HIV, with the aim of defining priorities and allocating resources. Existing governance mechanisms, such as health sector coordination committees, National AIDS Councils, or legislative bodies at national and subnational levels, can facilitate this dialogue. Consultative meetings may include focused discussions, and once the draft report is prepared, the findings should be presented to a wider group of stakeholders and interested parties. This can be achieved by circulating the review report and/or organizing informational meetings or workshops. The purpose of these meetings is to present preliminary findings and recommendations, gather feedback from key stakeholders, and consider the implications for subsequent planning processes. Such consultations provide an opportunity to validate the findings, receive additional input, build consensus on priorities and future directions, and enhance stakeholder participation and ownership. A dissemination plan should outline the processes for making the review reports and other relevant documentation accessible to all stakeholders. This includes specifying what information will be disseminated, to whom, for what purpose, and through which methods. Dissemination methods may include distributing paper or electronic copies of the report to relevant stakeholders, organizing workshops or consultative meetings, briefing decision-makers and implementers, and utilizing mass media (e.g., press releases and other forms of media coverage). Effective dissemination raises public and professional awareness of the program, increases the visibility of the recommendations, and enhances the likelihood of their implementation. Open discussions around the findings and recommendations can strengthen partnerships, generate new ideas, and foster enthusiasm for program improvements. The findings of the review should be used to improve program performance. This can be achieved through immediate implementation to enhance ongoing program delivery, such as improving service quality, better targeting of services to populations in greatest need, and addressing bottlenecks to scaling up services. The review may also inform reprogramming efforts, such as modifying program targets, redefining population groups, or switching to more effective interventions. Additionally, the review can serve as a foundation for developing a new strategy, providing context for building on past performance, selecting new priorities, and defining realistic targets. Demonstrating program results can also support resource mobilization by making a stronger case for continued or increased funding. Finally, program reviews enhance transparency and accountability, making programs more answerable to stakeholders. The process of formulating recommendations should be guided by key questions tailored to specific areas of the health sector response to HIV. These questions should be adapted to the review’s purpose and context. Key domains include antiretroviral therapy (ART), elimination of new HIV infections in children, HIV testing and counseling, HIV and tuberculosis co-management, services for people who inject drugs, services for sex workers, services for men who have sex with men and transgender individuals, condom promotion, male circumcision, human resources, strategic information, procurement and supply management, financing, leadership and governance, and community systems. For antiretroviral therapy, key considerations include whether treatment interventions are appropriate for the country’s epidemiological and socioeconomic context, whether policies and guidelines are up-to-date and aligned with international standards, whether adequate funding and human resources are available, and whether systems for drug and diagnostic access are sufficient. Metrics such as retention rates, viral suppression rates, and the distribution of ART services should also be evaluated. For the elimination of new HIV infections in children, the review should assess whether essential program elements are included, whether policies and guidelines are adequate, whether funding is sufficient, and whether information systems are in place to track progress. The quality, coverage, and accessibility of services should also be examined, along with the involvement of partners and the management of services. For HIV testing and counseling, the review should evaluate the adequacy of policies, strategies, and guidelines, the availability of trained personnel, the supply chain for HIV tests, and the appropriateness of service delivery models. Integration with other health services, the involvement of partners, and the management of services should also be assessed. Metrics such as the proportion of people living with HIV who know their status and the proportion of those referred to treatment or care services should be analyzed.
